title: Conservative interaction and path independence

units.content:
## 4. Conservative and Non-Conservative Forces

### Conservative Forces
A force is said to be **conservative** if:
1. The work done by it in moving a particle from one point to another depends **only on the initial and final positions**, and is independent of the path taken.
2. The work done by the force along any closed path is identically zero:
   $$\oint \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = 0$$

*Examples*: Gravitational force, electrostatic force, elastic spring force. All central forces are conservative.

### Non-Conservative Forces
If the work done by a force in moving a body between two points depends on the specific path followed, the force is **non-conservative**.
- The work done along a closed path is non-zero: $\oint \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} \ne 0$.
- Energy is dissipated into non-recoverable thermal, acoustic, or internal forms.

*Examples*: Frictional force, viscous drag.

### 7.1 Potential Energy

#### 7.1.1 Concept
Potential energy ($U$) is the energy possessed by a body or system by virtue of its position, configuration, or spatial state. It is independent of the dynamic trajectory by which the system arrived at that state.

Potential energy is intrinsically a relative quantity and requires the choice of a reference zero level ($U = 0$).

#### 7.1.2 Definition
$$\Delta U = U_B - U_A = -W_{c}(A \to B) = -\int_{A}^{B} \vec{F}_c \cdot d\vec{r}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Potential energy is defined **strictly for conservative forces**. It cannot be defined for non-conservative forces because their work depends on the path taken.
| WPE-N05 | §4 Conservative and non-conservative forces | WEP-04 Path independence | core; the closed-loop integral and curl form are beyond Grade 9 | 4 |

content.title: Conservative Forces & Path Independence
content.definition: A force is conservative if the work it performs along any path depends solely on the initial and final coordinates, which is mathematically equivalent to having zero curl and zero closed-loop line integral.
canonical_rules: Closed path invariant: oint F_c . dr = 0 for any closed contour.
In 2D Cartesian fields F = F_x i + F_y j, conservative condition requires dF_x/dy = dF_y/dx.
Path independence allows selecting the algebraically simplest integration path between two points.
operational_heuristics: Test partial derivative cross-symmetry: dF_x/dy == dF_y/dx.
If symmetric, compute work by path-independent potential difference: W = U(A) - U(B).
boundary_conditions: Friction / drag: oint f . dr < 0 (strictly non-conservative).

content.title: Potential energy belongs only to endpoint-determined interactions
content.badge_reason: It is tempting to hide every force inside an energy label, especially once gravitational potential energy is familiar.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish work contributions by sign and can reason about the net work over a path.
content.inferential_jump: Potential energy can replace the work bookkeeping for an interaction only when the relevant energy change is fixed by the endpoints; path-dependent friction must remain an explicit transfer.

teaching_path.action: Choose two routes between the same starting and ending heights and compare the gravitational energy change.
teaching_path.why_valid: If the endpoint change is the same for both routes, the account does not need the detailed path to determine that interaction's energy change.
teaching_path.output: route A: same start/end heights.  route B: same start/end heights.  gravitational potential-energy change: same.

teaching_path.action: Now add kinetic friction and compare a short route with a longer route between comparable endpoints.
teaching_path.why_valid: Friction acts along the travelled path, so changing path length changes its energy transfer even when endpoints are comparable.
teaching_path.output: short path -> smaller friction transfer.  longer path -> larger friction transfer.

teaching_path.action: Ask whether one endpoint-only energy label could predict both friction cases without knowing which path was taken.
teaching_path.why_valid: If two paths with comparable endpoints give different friction transfers, endpoint information alone cannot represent that interaction.
teaching_path.output: friction: path identity required; endpoint-only potential-energy replacement rejected.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every force can be assigned a potential energy so that its work can be hidden inside U.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can kinetic friction be represented by a single potential-energy difference that depends only on the start and finish positions?
misconceptions.repair: Use potential energy only for interactions whose energy change is fixed by endpoints; keep path-dependent friction as an explicit transfer.

exit_task.prompt: Two routes share the same start and finish heights. Gravity gives the same potential-energy change on both, while friction removes more energy on the longer route. Which interaction is eligible for endpoint-only potential-energy bookkeeping?

answer.summary: Gravity is eligible in this comparison; kinetic friction is not, because its transfer changes with the path.
reasoning: The gravitational potential-energy change is fixed by the shared endpoints.
The frictional transfer changes when the route length changes.
An endpoint-only account cannot represent a path-dependent interaction.
answer.check: Change the route while keeping the endpoints fixed; an eligible endpoint-only contribution stays the same while the frictional transfer need not.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer classifies interactions by endpoint versus path dependence and computes no energy value.

content.research_contribution: Author-created path-dependence discrimination; no potential-energy formula is asserted.

predict.prompt: Two paths start and end at the same heights, but one is much longer and rough. Before calculating, can one endpoint-only energy label represent the frictional transfer on both paths?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Friction depends on the travelled path, so comparable endpoints do not fix its transfer.

attempt.produces: A two-column classification of gravity and kinetic friction as endpoint-determined or path-dependent, supported by the two-route comparison.

rubric.criterion: Gravity is classified as endpoint-determined for the stated height comparison.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the unchanged start/end heights across routes.

rubric.criterion: Kinetic friction is classified as path-dependent.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing that route length changes the frictional transfer.

accepted: 'Gravity: endpoint-determined here. Friction: path-dependent, so keep its transfer explicit.'
rejected: 'Both get potential energy because both are forces.' This ignores the path test.

route.ask: If the start and finish heights are unchanged, what happens to the gravitational potential-energy change when the route bends?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the endpoint-only comparison using a familiar interaction.

route.ask: What changes for friction when the travelled route becomes longer?
route.why_this_ask: The contrasting interaction exposes path dependence.

route.ask: Could one endpoint-only label distinguish the short and long friction routes?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must test the proposed bookkeeping against two cases it would have to separate.

route.ask: Which interaction can therefore be replaced by an endpoint energy change in this comparison?
route.why_this_ask: The classification is produced from the path test rather than memorized as a list.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path gives the two-route comparisons. The learner route first establishes one endpoint-determined case, then breaks the same idea with friction and derives the eligibility rule.

boundary_test.prompt: Two different routes have the same start and finish but, by coincidence, friction removes the same amount of energy on both. Does that coincidence prove friction is endpoint-determined?
boundary_test.answer: No. A single matching pair does not remove the path dependence; changing the path can still change the frictional transfer.
boundary_test.confirms: Eligibility is about dependence on endpoints in general, not accidental equality in one example.

oracle.description: How this exit answer is stood behind. Exactly one of: `verification`, naming a subject validator and binding its inputs to declared data; `held_by`, naming the known issue that explains why no oracle exists yet; or `no_numeric_claim`, saying why the answer asserts no computed value. Silence is not an option, because the exit answer is what a learner measures themselves against.

predict.description: Pose the decision before revealing anything.

prompt.description: The decision, posed so a learner can commit to an answer.

defensible_answer.description: The answer that commitment is judged against. A prompt with no defensible answer is a musing, not a prediction.

attempt.description: What the learner produces, and how it closes without a tutor.

produces.description: What the learner should construct, draw, discriminate or explain.

closure.description: Which form of closure this attempt uses. Each value demands something the others do not, so that none is a synonym an author can pick to avoid work: MODEL_RESPONSE requires model_response, CRITERIA requires rubric, and RUBRIC requires rubric with accepted and rejected examples -- the spec's 'a rubric plus representative accepted and rejected answers', which is the stronger claim of the three.

model_response.description: Closure as one response, where one is right.

rubric.description: Closure as a rubric, where several responses are valid.

rejected.description: Representative responses it rejects. A rubric with no rejected example has not been tested against anything.

task.description: Schema 0.2.0: the concrete reconstruction task the learner performs (a body, givens, numbers or a situation). `produces` says what the attempt should contain; `task` is what the learner is asked to do. Rendered as the Core1B attempt.

representation_ref.description: The representation of this task's own situation (its bodies and values), shown with the Core1B attempt. When absent, Core1B falls back to the first construction unit's (Core1A) figure, which depicts a different situation.

stage_refs.description: Stages of representation_ref safe to show before the attempt; default is the first stage only.

reconstruct.description: The correct construction reached the way a learner would reach it. Held as questions rather than statements: teaching_path is the expert's summary, and a reconstruct route made of statements is that summary under a different key, which is exactly how this product became the declarative one.

route.description: The sequence of asks. Order is meaning: each one is answerable only once the previous has been answered.

ask.description: A question that moves the learner one decision forward. A sentence with a question mark on it is not an ask; the learner must be able to get it wrong.

why_this_ask.description: Why this question rather than another at this point. An author who cannot say this has ordered the route by the expert's convenience.

from_step_ref.description: The teaching_path step this ask arrives at, where one exists. Absent means the learner's route genuinely departs from the expert's, which is why both are held.

differs_from_teaching_path.description: How the learner's route differs from the expert's construction. This is the sentence a reviewer checks the A/B claim against, so it may not restate the teaching path it claims to differ from.

prompt.description: A limiting case, reversal or edge condition.

confirms.description: What passing it establishes, stated so that a recall question cannot be passed off as a boundary test.

answer.description: What passing it looks like. The shared closure invariant has no exception for the last prompt in a cycle.

compact_anchor.description: Schema 0.2.0: the Core1 compact anchor, a one-line instance of the governing relation that makes the map usable before Core1A.

representation_ref.description: The representation of this compact anchor's own situation, shown on the Core1 map. When absent, Core1 falls back to the microtopic's first representation_refs entry, which is often shared across microtopics.

role.description: What the step does to the state. A DECLARE step fixes a convention or a domain and legitimately produces no computation; a TRANSFORM step changes the mathematical state and must show the changed state, not describe it; a VERIFY step checks a result against something already established.

source_ref.description: The source this step's claim rests on. Absent means the step is the author's own construction, which is legitimate and is not the same as source-supported.
